questions.question: A supplier describes its single-use system in its catalog as "Ready-To-Use." According to the TR66 glossary, what is the nature of this term?

options.A: It is a marketing term with no regulatory or scientific basis and must be evaluated by the user
options.B: It is a regulatory-defined sterility grade, indicating the system has passed full sterility validation
options.C: It means the supplier has guaranteed all quality requirements, so the user is relieved of evaluation responsibility
options.D: It is an ISO-recognized designation indicating the system can be used in the process without verification

questions.explanation: The glossary states explicitly that Ready-To-Use is a marketing term with no regulatory or scientific basis, and the user must still perform their own evaluation. Treating it as a regulatory-defined sterility grade, a comprehensive supplier guarantee, or an ISO-recognized designation are common misunderstandings.

questions.question: Which statement about the difference between extractables and leachables is correct according to the TR66 glossary?

options.A: Extractables are substances that migrate under normal process conditions and can be detected in the final dosage form
options.B: Leachables are chemicals extracted under exaggerated conditions such as organic solvents and extreme temperatures
options.C: Extractables are extracted under exaggerated conditions and cover most, but not all, leachables
options.D: Leachables come only from non-product-contact materials and exclude migrants from product-contact materials

questions.explanation: The glossary defines extractables as substances extracted under exaggerated conditions such as organic solvents and high temperatures, which can represent most but not all potential leachables. Describing extractables as substances migrating under normal process conditions, or leachables as substances extracted under exaggerated conditions, reverses the two definitions; the statement that leachables come only from non-product-contact materials does not match the original text, "product-contact or non-product-contact."

questions.question: A user wants to extend the time or number of cycles a single-use system operates in a closed process without breaking the sterile barrier. What does the TR66 glossary call this practice?

options.A: Deployment, the actual operations of assembling and readying the system
options.B: Campaigning, extending use without breaking the sterile barrier
options.C: Closed System, an isolated system with no interaction with the outside environment
options.D: SUS Interchangeability, a functionally equivalent replacement SUS

questions.explanation: Campaigning refers to extending the period or number of cycles over which an SUS is used in a closed process without breaking the sterile barrier. Deployment is the hands-on assembly, and interchangeability is a replacement design; neither extends use.

questions.question: The Introduction of TR66 emphasizes that what condition ensures quality is no lower than that of traditional systems?

options.A: As long as specifications are stated in the purchase order, the supplier bears all responsibility for quality
options.B: Outsourcing all value-added operations to the supplier, so the user's quality system need not be involved
options.C: Comparing prices among multiple suppliers and choosing the lowest, to spread single-supplier risk
options.D: Establishing a formal partnership with the SUS supplier; a purchase order alone does not constitute a partnership

questions.explanation: The text states that only by establishing a formal partnership with the supplier can quality be ensured to be no lower than with traditional systems, and an effective control strategy covers the quality systems of both the supplier and the user. "Specifications in the purchase order make the supplier fully responsible" and "outsource all value-added operations" both shift responsibility unilaterally to the supplier.

questions.question: In the TR66 glossary, what is the relationship between Technical Diligence and the quality audit program?

options.A: It completely replaces the quality audit; once technical diligence is complete, the supplier no longer needs to be audited
options.B: It supplements the quality audit, verifying the technical capability of the SUS and supplier and the fit, and is ongoing
options.C: It is performed only once before signing the purchase contract and need not be repeated for routine purchasing afterward
options.D: It is dedicated to assessing the supplier's financial stability and has nothing to do with the technical capability of the SUS

questions.explanation: The glossary states that technical diligence is used to verify the technical capability and fit of the SUS and supplier, complements the quality audit, and runs through implementation and subsequent routine purchasing. "Completely replaces the quality audit" and "performed only once before signing" both contradict the text.

questions.question: TR66 §3.0 proposes a gated approach for preparing a manufacturing strategy. What is the intent of its gates and overall design?

options.A: To require each stage to be completed in linear order, with no gate skipped and no entry partway through
options.B: To assess all risks at once at the final stage of the decision, with the overall decision reviewed only once
options.C: To weigh pros and cons with scientific and risk assessment at decision points, terminating early if major problems cannot be resolved
options.D: To review only financial benefit, with technical feasibility and patient safety outside the scope of evaluation

questions.explanation: A gate is a decision point at which the pros and cons are weighed on a scientific and risk basis, with the aim of terminating quickly if major problems cannot be resolved. The text also says the decision path need not be linear and users may enter at any point, so the statement "each stage in linear order, no entry partway through" is wrong.

questions.question: TR66 §3.0 notes that the weighting of decision areas varies by user. Which pairing matches the examples in the text?

options.A: A CMO values shortening changeover time, whereas a large pharmaceutical company weighs the risk of new technology against use of existing equipment
options.B: A CMO values reducing the risk of new technology, whereas a large pharmaceutical company values shortening changeover time between different products
options.C: A CMO values the capital investment in large fixed MUS, whereas a large pharmaceutical company values reducing labor and resources
options.D: Their weighing factors are exactly the same, and the text holds that organization type does not affect the weighting of the areas

questions.explanation: The text gives the example that a contract manufacturer may value shorter changeover between products, while a large pharmaceutical company may weigh the risk of adopting new technology against the use of existing capabilities. The option that swaps the emphases of the CMO and the large pharmaceutical company reverses them; "their weighing factors are exactly the same" is the opposite of weighting by circumstance.

questions.question: How does TR66 §3.1 recommend that a user's method of judging the technical feasibility of an SUS be documented?

options.A: In a risk analysis document consistent with ICH Q9, including the factors that influence the design
options.B: Verbally in project meetings only, because feasibility assessment is not a GMP activity requiring documentation
options.C: By replacing the user's own risk assessment and records with the supplier's catalog and specifications
options.D: By including it in the annual product quality review and replacing individual project assessments with the ICH Q10 approach

questions.explanation: The text requires the approach to technical feasibility to be documented in a risk analysis document consistent with ICH Q9, including factors that influence the design such as process compatibility, component reliability, and facility design.

questions.question: What does TR66 §3.2 recommend regarding the economic analysis before adopting an SUS?

options.A: Perform the analysis after implementation is complete, calibrating expected benefits with actual operating data
options.B: It should be built into the high-level manufacturing strategy from the beginning, and a simplified model is sufficient for preliminary decisions
options.C: It is needed only for new buildings (greenfield); retrofits of existing facilities do not need analysis
options.D: A highly detailed, complete model must be built before deciding; simplified models cannot be used

questions.explanation: §3.2 states that any significant decision requires an economic analysis, preferably as part of the high-level manufacturing strategy from the outset; a simplified model is generally sufficient when deciding preliminarily whether to consider an SUS.

questions.question: What approach does TR66 §3.3.1 recommend for assessing the effect of an SUS on leachables in the process?

options.A: Simply assume the materials do not leach, and test only at final product release
options.B: Replace extractables studies with product stability study results, since the two have the same purpose
options.C: First conduct an extractables study to identify leachables, then investigate further if there are concerns
options.D: Use only the supplier's promotional materials, with no study or follow-up assessment needed

questions.explanation: The text describes two steps: first use an extractables study to identify potential leachables, then, if materials of concern are found, perform further studies. The other options all omit the extractables study.

questions.question: TR66 §4.3 mentions that an SUS must be manufactured and assembled in a clean environment. What cleanliness classification is typical for the assembly room?

options.A: ISO 5 (Grade A), with all operations under unidirectional airflow
options.B: ISO 7 or ISO 8 (approximately Grade B/C or Grade C/D)
options.C: An ISO 9 ordinary environment, with only personnel entry and exit controlled
options.D: ISO 6, sharing the same air conditioning system as the main production area

questions.explanation: The text states that the assembly room is typically ISO 7 or 8 (corresponding to Grade B/C or C/D), with routine non-viable particle and microbial sampling. ISO 5 would be excessive, and an ordinary environment would be insufficient.

questions.question: An MUS can be cleaned internally by CIP after assembly, but an SUS must be manufactured and assembled in a clean environment. What reason does TR66 §4.3 give?

options.A: Because there is no practical method for cleaning an SU assembly after it is assembled
options.B: Because the plastic materials of an SUS cannot withstand gamma irradiation at all
options.C: Because regulations require all SUS assembly to be performed in an ISO 5 environment
options.D: Because an SUS must be cleaned by CIP before use, but this tends to leave residues

questions.explanation: The text says an SUS must be manufactured and assembled in a clean environment because there is no practical cleaning method for an SU assembly. "Plastic materials cannot withstand gamma irradiation" is the opposite of the text (gamma irradiation is commonly used for sterilization), and "always in an ISO 5 environment" does not match the ISO 7/8 statement.

questions.question: Under TR66 §4.4, after which activity should the technical feasibility assessment be performed?

options.A: After the supplier delivers and installation qualification (IQ) is complete
options.B: After the process validation report is completed and approved, to confirm actual operating results
options.C: After a complete extractables report is obtained and signed off by the supplier
options.D: After producing the URS describing the technical requirements of the specific SUS application

questions.explanation: §4.4 states that the feasibility assessment is performed after the URS is produced, to demonstrate that the proposed SUS can meet the functional and regulatory requirements of the specific application. IQ, the validation report, and the extractables report are all later outputs and cannot serve as the starting point for the assessment.

questions.question: CFF (TFF) devices come in two constructions: flat-sheet cassettes and hollow fiber cartridges. According to TR66 §4.11, which can currently be classified as an SU filter device?

options.A: Only flat-sheet cassettes, because their disposable design is more mature
options.B: Both flat-sheet cassettes and hollow-fiber cartridges have been classified as SU devices
options.C: Only hollow-fiber cartridges
options.D: Neither format can be classified; TFF must still always use fixed systems

questions.explanation: §4.11 states explicitly that currently only hollow-fiber cartridges can be classified as SU filter devices. Counting cassettes as well, or denying both, does not match the text.

questions.question: Why does TR66 §4.14 emphasize that a failure at final fill has an especially large impact?

options.A: Because downstream of this stage there is no way to reduce the impact of a quality failure
options.B: Because several purification steps remain after filling that can remedy it and remove contaminants
options.C: Because final fill uses no single-use components and therefore lacks control
options.D: Because final fill is always performed in an unprotected open environment, which is extremely risky

questions.explanation: §4.14 states that a final fill failure has a large impact because later processing cannot reduce a quality failure. Ways to reduce the risk include an aseptic environment, physical barriers isolating the operator from the process, and validating the sterility of process components.

questions.question: An SUS supplier wants to establish or extend the shelf life of an SUS. Under TR66 §5.9.1, which type of study provides the most reliable evidence?

options.A: Estimating from sterilization dose records, with no separate aging study required
options.B: Relying only on the supplier's written statement, with the user not needing to review any data
options.C: Mainly accelerated aging studies, since they are superior to real-time studies in all circumstances
options.D: Real-time aging, with accelerated aging substituted only when real-time is not possible

questions.explanation: §5.9.1 states that real-time aging provides the best data; if it cannot be performed, accelerated studies are an appropriate substitute, and extending shelf life must be supported by relevant data.

questions.question: Mold release agents and resin additives of an SUS (such as calcium stearate) may be derived from tallow. How does TR66 §5.7 view their BSE/TSE risk?

options.A: They are high-risk animal-derived components that must always be completely avoided in SUS and tested lot by lot
options.B: The risk is low; they are not specified BSE risk materials listed in 21 CFR 189.5
options.C: The risk is equivalent to high-risk animal tissue, and all lots must complete infectivity testing and be released before use
options.D: The text holds that tallow derivatives cannot occur in plastic resins or mold release agents, so no assessment is needed

questions.explanation: §5.7 explains that the BSE/TSE risk of SUS is low; tallow-derived additives are not considered specified BSE risk materials under 21 CFR 189.5, and EMA 410/01 also notes that after rigorous processing they are unlikely to be infectious.

questions.question: TR66 §5.10.1 states that SUS are particularly well suited to sterilization by irradiation. What is the main reason?

options.A: Radiation has no effect on plastics at all, so the dose can be raised freely without evaluation
options.B: Plastics fully absorb ionizing radiation, so only the outer layer needs treatment to ensure the interior is sterile
options.C: Plastics are relatively transparent to ionizing radiation, so complex systems can be sterilized and no sterilant is spread into the fluid path
options.D: Radiation removes all extractables at the same time, so no extraction study is needed later

questions.explanation: The reason in §5.10.1 is that plastics are relatively transparent to ionizing radiation, so complex systems can be sterilized without spreading sterilant into the fluid path, and it is suitable for plastics that cannot withstand steam. The other options have no basis in the text.

questions.question: When auditing an SUS supplier, which item does TR66 §5.4.1 identify as unique to SUS and one that should be included in the audit?

options.A: Review only the marketing materials and catalogs the supplier provides, without examining any procedures or records
options.B: The supplier's definition of change, its change-control process, and customer notification
options.C: No need to evaluate the supplier's particle control and reduction program during the audit, because particles are irrelevant to SUS
options.D: Only confirm that the supplier holds an ISO certificate, without reviewing complaint handling and the quality system

questions.explanation: §5.4.1 states that the items unique to an SUS audit include the supplier's definition of change, the operation of change control, and customer notification, and that its particle control and reduction program should be evaluated. The statement that there is "no need to evaluate the particle control and reduction program" is the opposite of the text.

questions.question: Which statement about the reuse of SUS in TR66 §5.12 is correct?

options.A: Reuse is possible only in a few exceptions, and the effect on the batch definition must be considered
options.B: Reuse is the normal practice for SUS, and users need not consider the effect on the batch definition
options.C: As long as the supplier agrees, any SUS can be reused an unlimited number of times, with no further evaluation of quality requirements
options.D: Any reuse is expressly prohibited, even for storage containers whose connections have not been broken

questions.explanation: §5.12 explains that SUS are designed to be single-use, but in a few cases (such as a mixing container or storage tank for buffer concentrate, with connections not interrupted) they may be reused; the user must evaluate quality requirements themselves and consider whether the batch definition is affected.

questions.question: What scope does the lifecycle approach described in TR66 §6.2 cover when assessing cost?

options.A: Only the purchase price of consumables and disposable components, excluding other cost items
options.B: Only operating expenses in the production phase, excluding setup and decommissioning costs
options.C: Only the initial capital investment, because the remaining costs differ little between options
options.D: Initial capital investment, production and quality overheads, and decommissioning

questions.explanation: §6.2 explains that the lifecycle approach assesses costs over the entire life of the project, including initial capital investment, production and quality overheads, and decommissioning, and incorporates time and risk factors.

questions.question: When TR66 §6.5 evaluates the feasibility of an SUS project quantitatively, which metric is the main basis?

options.A: The purchase price of a single piece of equipment, irrespective of batch quantity and capacity
options.B: Annual net profit after tax, with no need to consider the cost structure of each batch
options.C: The company's total headcount, as the sole basis for estimating the capacity of each option
options.D: Average batch cost

questions.explanation: §6.5 states that quantitative evaluation can examine the feasibility of an SUS project based on average batch cost, with multiple submodels combined into an overall economic model.

questions.question: TR66 §6.6 notes that an SUS may produce more batches per year than an MUS. What is the main reason?

options.A: SUS batch process times are longer, which increases the annual production schedule available
options.B: SUS batch sizes are necessarily larger, so more batches are needed per year
options.C: SUS shorten the time required for changeover
options.D: SUS eliminate all release and quality testing procedures, making each batch process shorter

questions.explanation: §6.6 explains that an SUS may produce more batches per year because it shortens changeover time; average batch cost is also affected by fixed costs and the number of batches. None of the other options is supported by the text.

questions.question: SUS-based facility projects usually have shorter timelines. Under TR66 §6.11.1, how does this advantage translate into commercial benefit?

options.A: Capital investment can be deferred or time to market accelerated, and deferring investment also reduces the risk of a bad investment
options.B: It affects only construction cost, with no effect on the launch timeline or exclusivity-period revenue
options.C: The text holds that MUS facilities usually have shorter timelines, so SUS has no timeline advantage
options.D: The only value of a shorter timeline is reducing construction labor, unrelated to the timing of investment

questions.explanation: §6.11.1 states that SUS facility projects have significantly shorter timelines, which allows capital investment to be deferred (reducing the cost of capital and, because more clinical data are available, the risk of a bad investment) or the product to reach the market sooner, effectively lengthening the exclusivity period under patent protection.

questions.question: TR66 §6.13 states that recycling SU materials is currently not commercially viable. What is the reason?

options.A: Regulations expressly prohibit recycling any plastic material that has been used in drug manufacture
options.B: SU materials are made entirely of metal, and their recycling value is far below the cost of recovery
options.C: Recycling applies only to fixed equipment, and by definition SU materials cannot be recycled
options.D: Biohazardous waste may need to be inactivated or components separated, and volumes are often insufficient to justify a program

questions.explanation: §6.13 states that biohazardous waste may need to be inactivated or multi-component assemblies separated, and the total volume of waste is often insufficient to support a recycling program, so it is currently not commercially viable.

questions.question: How many gateways and stages make up the SUS implementation road map in TR66 §7.1?

options.A: G1 to G5, and S1 to S5
options.B: G1 to G10, and S1 to S10
options.C: G1 to G8, and S1 to S7
options.D: G1 to G7, and S1 to S8

questions.explanation: §7.1 explains that the road map consists of gateways G1 to G8 and stages S1 to S7, with specific objectives to be met before each gateway before proceeding to the next.

questions.question: In the SUS implementation S4 (Business Case) stage, what is the main document output?

options.A: Project execution plan
options.B: The complete equipment OQ report and process validation report
options.C: The personnel training plan and completed, signed-off training records
options.D: The supplier's annual audit report and all change notifications

questions.explanation: §7.4 states that the main document output of S4 is the PEP, which includes facility and process integration, technical investigation, supplier selection, and supply chain. OQ, training, and the like belong to later stages.

questions.question: In the S5 (Development) stage, the project team wants to place a purchase order with the supplier first, but the user requirements are not complete. What is TR66 §7.5's position?

options.A: A purchase order may be placed first, with user requirements completed after the equipment is delivered
options.B: As long as the user requirements for the SU part are complete, the MU part can be completed later
options.C: User requirements and the purchasing process are unrelated, so their order need not be considered
options.D: Complete user requirements should precede the procurement process (such as commercial negotiation or placing a purchase order)

questions.explanation: §7.5 requires complete user requirements to precede the procurement process (for example, commercial negotiation with a strategic partner or placing a purchase order). Ordering first and completing later, or purchasing after completing only the SU requirements, both violate this sequence.

questions.question: Which statement about TR66 §7.3.8's position on reuse of SU components is correct?

options.A: Reuse of SU components is encouraged to reduce cost, with the same number of cycles recommended for every component
options.B: Reuse is not recommended; an SU chromatography column can be campaigned, but SU tubing may need to be replaced every cycle
options.C: Both SU tubing and SU chromatography columns can withstand multiple caustic cycles, so they can always be reused
options.D: Reuse is not permitted under any circumstances, and the text does not accept repeated filling within a single campaign

questions.explanation: §7.3.8 states that reuse of SUS is not recommended and that a position should be established in advance from a risk perspective; an SU column can be taken through multiple caustic cycles to process several pools, but SU tubing may not withstand this and would need replacing every time.

questions.question: What consequence does TR66 §7.2.1 identify for poor stakeholder management?

options.A: Divergent implementation directions and missed opportunities for standardization (for example, multiple connectors in parallel)
options.B: Suppliers will automatically lower prices, because the user's requirements become clearer
options.C: No effect on project outcomes, because stakeholder management concerns only administrative communication
options.D: Implementation costs necessarily decrease, because different departments each choose the most suitable SUS

questions.explanation: §7.2.1 states that poor management leads to divergent implementation directions and missed opportunities for standardization and process streamlining, for example when multiple SUS technologies or suppliers run in parallel and each uses a different sterile connector or storage bag.

questions.question: According to the text, what is the nature of the example user requirements document in TR66 Appendix I?

options.A: A final, unalterable contract document; once signed, no requirement or scope may be adjusted
options.B: A living document that can be updated as the project progresses, written by the user or sponsor
options.C: A document that can be written only by the equipment supplier, with the user only reviewing and signing off, not editing it
options.D: A validated document in which all requirements have been confirmed through qualification

questions.explanation: Appendix I states that such a document should be treated as a living document that can be updated as the project progresses, and that its author may be the user or its sponsor; the requirements in the example may also not yet have been qualified and are only the basis of the design.

questions.topic: Biosafety level in the URS example
questions.question: The Appendix I example builds a new production suite for a viral-particle gene therapy injectable. To which biosafety level should it be designed?

options.A: BSL1
options.B: BSL3
options.C: BSL2
options.D: BSL4

questions.explanation: §8.2.1 states that the new production suite should be designed to biosafety level 2 (BSL2), in compliance with the relevant EU requirements.

questions.question: In the Appendix I example, how should floor and process drains in the manufacturing area (including product-containing wastewater and elution buffers) be handled?

options.A: Discharged directly to the public drainage system and treated together at the municipal sewage plant with no separate inactivation
options.B: Held temporarily in open drainage channels and collected together during a monthly scheduled operation for off-site treatment
options.C: Discharged first into the general sewage system, with inactivation performed separately off-site afterward
options.D: Routed through closed connections to a collection tank, chemically or thermally inactivated, and neutralized before discharge

questions.explanation: §8.2.4.4 requires drains to be routed to the collection tanks of an inactivation system (closed connections), inactivated chemically or thermally in the balance tanks, and neutralized before being moved to the public drain.

questions.question: In the Appendix I example, which standards are followed for the design of the cleanrooms and for their validation, operation, and monitoring, respectively?

options.A: Designed to ISO 14644-1, but validated, operated, and monitored per EU GMP and PIC/S
options.B: Designed per EU GMP and PIC/S, but validated, operated, and monitored to ISO 14644-1
options.C: Design, validation, operation, and monitoring all solely to ISO 14644-1, with no GMP requirements involved
options.D: Designed per ICH Q9, and validated, operated, and monitored per 21 CFR Part 211

questions.explanation: §8.4.3.1 states that the cleanrooms are designed to ISO 14644-1 but validated, operated, and monitored per EU GMP and PIC/S. The option that reverses the two (designed to GMP, validated to ISO) is wrong; "everything solely to ISO 14644-1" and "designed per ICH Q9, handled per 21 CFR Part 211" do not match the text.

questions.question: In the Appendix I example, what are the two main purposes of the personnel airlocks?

options.A: Keeping the clean area under negative pressure to prevent outward leakage, and letting all personnel share a single route
options.B: Keeping the clean area under positive pressure to isolate rooms, and letting office and production personnel share a changing room
options.C: Maintaining positive pressure to separate rooms, and preventing contaminants from the BSL2 active area from spreading to the clean area
options.D: Only controlling temperature and humidity in the area, with no pressure differential management or prevention of contaminant spread

questions.explanation: §8.2.6.2 states that the first objective of the airlocks is to maintain positive pressure in the clean area and separate rooms, and the second is to prevent contaminants from BSL2 active rooms from spreading to the cleaner non-active areas; personnel flow in the active area should be one-way.

questions.question: In the Appendix II PEP example, in addition to the spare parts needed for commissioning, testing, and qualification, for how long will SEC also supply critical spare parts?

options.A: 6 months from the installation date
options.B: 1 year from the installation date
options.C: 5 years from the installation date
options.D: 2 years from the installation date

questions.explanation: §9.4.4.2 specifies that SEC will supply the spare parts needed for commissioning, testing, and qualification, and critical spare parts for two years from the installation date.

questions.question: In the Appendix II PEP example, how is the supply of consumables such as filters, gaskets, lubricants, and bags divided?

options.A: All supplied by Company X, with SEC responsible for no consumables
options.B: SEC supplies them until the end of commissioning, and Company X supplies them thereafter
options.C: SEC supplies them until the end of OQ, and thereafter SEC continues to supply them until project closure
options.D: All supplied by SEC permanently, including routine production consumables after the project ends

questions.explanation: §9.4.4.3 specifies that SEC supplies the consumables needed up to the end of commissioning, and Company X provides consumables thereafter.

questions.question: In the Appendix II PEP example, the basic design document becomes the project baseline once reviewed and approved by Company X. How should a deviation from this baseline be handled?

options.A: Handled per the change management procedure
options.B: SEC engineers judge and adjust it themselves, notifying Company X afterward
options.C: Based on verbal agreement between the parties, with no formal document or written procedure needed
options.D: Collected after OQ is complete, with the final as-built drawings replacing the change procedure

questions.explanation: §9.4.3 states that the basic design document constitutes the project baseline, and any deviation must be handled through the change management procedure, with the steering committee overseeing scope and schedule.

questions.question: In the Appendix II PEP example, what are the responsibilities of the joint SEC and Company X steering committee?

options.A: Directing day-to-day site construction and equipment installation and directly managing subcontractor staff
options.B: Replacing SEC's quality control and performing the IQ and OQ testing of all equipment
options.C: Ensuring project objectives are met, approving the PEP, schedule and planning, and the monthly project report
options.D: Only procuring spare parts and consumables, without taking part in project risk handling or progress oversight

questions.explanation: §9.2.6 lists the steering committee's responsibilities, including ensuring project objectives are met, establishing a shared understanding of risk handling, approving the PEP and the schedule and economic planning, overseeing progress, and approving the monthly report.

questions.question: In the Appendix II PEP example, within how long after the start of basic design do the project objectives require OQ of the manufacturing suite to be completed?

options.A: Within 12 months
options.B: Within 18 months
options.C: Within 24 months
options.D: Within 36 months

questions.explanation: One of the project objectives in §9.2.4 is to complete OQ of the manufacturing suite within 18 months after the start of basic design.

questions.question: In the Appendix III SUS implementation training plan, what are the type and duration of the training module "Bioreactor Bags: reception and storage"?

options.A: EXT, 2 hours
options.B: EXT, 4 hours
options.C: INT, 2 hours
options.D: INT, 4 hours

questions.explanation: The Appendix III training table lists the reception and storage module for Bioreactor Bags as INT (internal training), 2 hours, for Warehousing.
questions.reference: PDA TR66 §10.0 Appendix III, SUS Implementation Training Plan

questions.question: In the Appendix III training table, which pair of modules are both INT (internal training)?

options.A: Calibration and Qualification, and SUS Integrity and Leak Testing
options.B: SUS Bioreactor Utilization 1, and SUS Bioreactor Utilization 2
options.C: Bioreactor Bags: preparation and integration, and Calibration and Qualification
options.D: Bioreactor Bags: reception and storage, and SUS Disposal

questions.explanation: The only modules marked INT in the table are reception and storage and SUS Disposal, both 2 hours; the remaining modules (such as Calibration and Qualification and SUS Integrity and Leak Testing) are EXT, 4 hours.
questions.reference: PDA TR66 §10.0 Appendix III, SUS Implementation Training Plan

questions.question: Which department or role is listed in the Approvals (Date/Signature) field of the Appendix III training plan?

options.A: Qualified Person
options.B: Regulatory Affairs
options.C: Procurement
options.D: Engineering

questions.explanation: The sign-off fields in Appendix III include Manufacturing, Quality, Qualified Person, Human Resources, and Finance; Regulatory Affairs, Procurement, and Engineering are not listed.
questions.reference: PDA TR66 §10.0 Appendix III, SUS Implementation Training Plan

questions.question: Which ICH guideline is reference number 5 in TR66 §11.0?

options.A: Q9: Quality Risk Management (2005)
options.B: Q10: Pharmaceutical Quality Systems (2008)
options.C: Q8(R2): Pharmaceutical Development (2009)
options.D: Q7: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for APIs (2000)

questions.explanation: The references run in order: 1 Q6A, 2 Q7, 3 Q8(R2), 4 Q9, 5 Q10, 6 Q11; item 5 is Q10 Pharmaceutical Quality Systems (2008).

questions.question: What is the subject of ICH Q7 (2000), reference number 2 in TR66 §11.0?

options.A: Quality Risk Management
options.B: Pharmaceutical Development: Technical Requirements for Registration
options.C: Specifications: Test Procedures and Acceptance Criteria for New Drug Substance
options.D: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients

questions.explanation: Reference 2 is ICH Q7: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (2000). Quality Risk Management is Q9, Pharmaceutical Development is Q8(R2), and Specifications is Q6A.
